newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. assures Kuwait of security commitment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. assures Kuwait of security commitment.

text.p: The United States Monday assured Kuwait of Washington's firm commitment to its security and to containing former occupier Iraq and neighboring Iran.
U.S. Defense Secretary William Cohen told a news conference "I can summarise the United States policy toward Kuwait in three words: commitment, cooperation and containment."
His Kuwaiti counterpart Sheikh Salem Sabah al-Salem al-Sabah told the conference he explained to Cohen "how satisfied we are with the existing relationship, training and cooperation."

Cohen, who arrived in Kuwait Sunday as part of a five-nation Gulf Arab familiarisation tour, earlier Monday held "very fruitful and interesting" talks with Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah, Sheikh Salem said.
Cohen said the United States would continue to maintain a strong military presence in the oil-rich region to deter threats from Iraq and Iran, the Gulf's two main military powers.

He said despite recent calls by some states to ease U.N. sanctions against Iraq, the United States favoured maintaining them until Baghdad complied with all 1990-91 Gulf crisis-related U.N. resolutions.
U.S. forces led an international military coalition in the 1991 Gulf War to end Iraq's seven-month occupation of Kuwait.

Cohen said U.S. policy toward Iran would not change unless Tehran showed a marked shift from its alleged support for "terrorism," keeness to buy and develop more weapons and end its undermining of the Middle East peace process.

Washington believes Iran poses a threat to its neighbors with its wide variety of weapons from China and Russia and eagerness to buy new missiles with even greater range and more lethal capability, Cohen said.
He said Iran had chemical arms under development and possibly also biological weapons while it sought to develop a nuclear capability "sometime into the future."
"We have to be concerned in terms of what the goals and designs of Iran are. Do they pose a threat to the region? We believe that they do," Cohen added.

Iran often denies supporting international "terrorism" and stresses that its nuclear program is for peaceful uses. It also says its defense spending is far less than that of its neighbors although it has a much larger population and territory to defend.

"We have seen little evidence of that (change) to date. So if there is going to be change as reflected by the most recent elections that the people of Iran wish to have change, then I think everyone in the region, as well the United States, would welcome that," Cohen added.
Last month's presidential election of Mohammad Khatami, seen as a moderate Iranian leader, raised hopes that Tehran would soften its policy toward the West. He assumes office in August.
